problem: mmWave AoA-based target localization is unreliable for navigation because the strongest path is often NLOS with many reflections, and prior link-state classifiers only do binary LOS/NLOS from aggregate features, ignoring multi-array and beam-sweeping mmWave front-ends.
motivation: In search-and-rescue-style tasks a robot must find a wireless-emitting target in an unknown environment. Following the angle of arrival is only useful when the strongest path is LOS or a single reflection, so the agent must know which case it is in and otherwise fall back to exploration.
key_idea: Estimate mmWave multipath parameters with a beam-sweeping low-rank tensor decomposition, classify the link state (LOS / first-order NLOS / higher-order NLOS / outage) with a small neural net, and override the Active Neural-SLAM goal with the AoA only when the state is LOS or first-order NLOS.
insight: Distinguishing first-order from higher-order NLOS matters: AoA error on the strongest path is small for LOS (98% under 5°) and first-order NLOS (85% under 5°), but over 40% of higher-order NLOS errors exceed 10°. Navigation ablations show that following AoA based on SNR only gets stuck in 11% of moderate and 23% of hard tests, and the LOS-only policy is worse than the LOS-or-first-order policy. The classifier trained on raw multipath features generalizes to unseen buildings.
method: Beam-sweeping double-directional path estimation: TX sweeps codewords over 3 arrays, and RX correlates over delay, RX angle and TX beam to form a 3rd-order tensor. Two-way PCA low-rank decomposition gives per-path relative delay, AoA, AoD and SNR.
Multi-array antenna model: 3 arrays at 0°/±120° on both UE (1x8 ULA, 24 beams) and gNB (4x4 UPA, 48 beams) with patch element patterns, no LO sync across arrays, 28 GHz, 400 MHz bandwidth, 23 dBm.

Link-state classifier: fully connected net with hidden layers of 8 and 6 units and a 4-way softmax. Input is the scaled raw features (angles, SNR, relative delay) of the K=5 strongest paths (20 inputs, or 15 without AoD). Adam, lr 0.001, 300 epochs, batch 1024.
Wireless dataset: 38 Gibson floors simplified to 2D floor plans, ray traced with Remcom Wireless InSite at 28 GHz, 10 random TX positions each, on a 160x160 RX grid at 0.15 m spacing.

Navigation integration: the strongest-path AoA becomes the wireless navigation goal in Active Neural-SLAM when the state is LOS or first-order NLOS and SNR > 10 dB. Otherwise the agent uses the Global Policy exploration goal, then Fast Marching planning and the local policy.

Baselines and evaluation: an oracle that knows the TX location, and 'Visual LOS CV-Based SLAM' (explore, then go straight to the target once seen, assumed 100% detection). Evaluated on 193 tests across 20 held-out maps, split into easy/moderate/hard (52/76/65).

setting.backbone: Small 2-hidden-layer MLP link-state classifier (trained from scratch) + PCA tensor decomposition + Active Neural-SLAM (pretrained global/local policies, Neural-SLAM module)
setting.training_data: Ray-traced 28 GHz links from 18 Gibson environments (483,690 TX-RX links; 10 TX each); tested on 20 other environments (563,810 links)
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB + pose readings for Neural-SLAM, plus mmWave multipath estimates (AoA, AoD, relative delay, SNR) from beam-sweeping signals
setting.action_space: Habitat low-level navigation actions driven by long-term goals and a Fast Marching planner (short-term goal within 0.25 m)
setting.simulator: AI Habitat with Gibson; Remcom Wireless InSite ray tracing
setting.privileged: None for the proposed method (the oracle baseline knows the TX location; ground-truth ray tracing is used only for classifier labels in training)

numbers_note: Navigation results are shown only in figures (arrival success rate and arrival-time CDFs by difficulty), not in tables; the only numeric text results are link-state classification accuracy and AoA error percentages, which are not standard navigation benchmarks.
results: The link-state classifier reaches about 88% validation accuracy on 20 unseen environments, versus 84% for a modified prior method (Huang et al.); removing AoD lowers LOS accuracy from 96% to 88%. In navigation, the LOS-or-first-order-NLOS policy has the highest arrival success rate at all difficulty levels and beats the vision-only Visual LOS CV-Based SLAM baseline. It has the fastest arrival on moderate and hard tests and comes close to the oracle.
limitations: Wireless and visual data are not fused: the agent uses one or the other at each step, and wireless information is not used for SLAM.

Simulation only: 2D floor plans, a single wall material, 28 GHz ray tracing, and assumed TX beam-angle knowledge; no real robot experiments, and quantitative navigation results appear only in figures.
Requires TX/RX synchronization and codebook knowledge for AoD; the AoA-only variant is notably worse.
builds_on: Low-rank tensor decomposition mmWave channel estimation (Zhou et al., Wen et al.)
Huang et al. ML LOS/NLOS identification
